higher-order Greeks.def: Measures of how the first-order Greeks themselves change as the underlying's price, time or volatility moves. Vanna, charm, volga, speed and color are the five that matter most for dealer flow.

vanna.def: The rate at which an option's delta changes as implied volatility changes, which equals the rate at which its vega changes as the underlying's price moves. It is negative for out-of-the-money puts.

charm.def: The rate at which an option's delta changes as time passes, with the underlying's price and implied volatility unchanged. It runs on calendar time, weekends included.

volga.def: The rate at which an option's vega changes as implied volatility changes, also called vomma. It is positive for options away from the strike, so a long option gains faster than vega alone predicts when volatility rises.

speed.def: The rate at which an option's gamma changes as the underlying's price moves: the third derivative of the option's value with respect to that price.

color.def: The rate at which an option's gamma changes as time passes. It is positive near the strike, where gamma grows toward expiry, and negative far from it, where gamma drains away.

volatility point.def: One percentage point of annualized volatility, as in a move from 20% to 21% implied volatility. Also called a vol point.

variance swap.def: A contract that pays the difference between the variance an asset's returns actually show over a period and a variance level agreed at the start.

straddle.def: A position of a call and a put on the same underlying with the same strike and expiry. Buying one is a bet on a large move either way; selling one is a bet that the underlying stays near the strike.

rule of 16.def: A shortcut that divides an annualized volatility by 16, close to the square root of 252 trading days, to give the one-standard-deviation daily move it implies. A VIX of 16 prices a 1% day.

close-to-close estimator.def: The simplest estimate of realized volatility: the average squared log return from one day's close to the next. It ignores everything that happens within each day.

Parkinson estimator.def: A realized-volatility estimate built from each day's high-low range, published by Parkinson in 1980. It needs far fewer days than the close-to-close estimate for the same precision, but it misses overnight gaps.

Garman-Klass estimator.def: A realized-volatility estimate, published in 1980, that uses each day's open, high, low and close. It is more efficient than the Parkinson estimator but still misses overnight gaps.

Yang-Zhang estimator.def: A realized-volatility estimate, published in 2000, that combines the overnight move, the open-to-close move and a drift-adjusted range term, so that it handles overnight gaps.

implied volatility surface.def: Implied volatility as a function of both strike and expiry. Its shape across strikes is the skew, and its shape across expiries is the term structure.

volatility skew.def: The pattern of implied volatility across strikes at one expiry. In equity index options, out-of-the-money puts carry higher implied volatility than out-of-the-money calls.

term structure.def: How implied volatility varies with time to expiry for the same underlying. It is in contango when longer-dated volatility is higher, and in backwardation when shorter-dated volatility is higher.

contango.def: A term structure in which longer-dated prices or implied volatilities sit above shorter-dated ones. It is the usual shape for equity implied volatility.

backwardation.def: A term structure in which shorter-dated prices or implied volatilities sit above longer-dated ones. For equity implied volatility it is a mark of stress.

SKEW index.def: A Cboe index, published since 1990, that condenses the steepness of the 30-day SPX skew into one number. Higher values mean heavier demand for crash protection.

put-call parity.def: The identity that ties the price of a European call to the price of the European put with the same strike and expiry: the call minus the put equals the underlying's price minus the present value of the strike. If it fails, a riskless profit is available.

synthetic position.def: A combination of options, the underlying and cash that has the same payoff as a different position, such as a long call and a short put at one strike, which together act like owning the underlying.

gap risk.def: The risk that the underlying opens at a price well away from its previous close, so that a position held overnight or over a weekend takes the whole jump with no chance to trade out.

borrow cost.def: The fee a short seller pays to borrow the shares sold, quoted as an annual rate. It can be very high for stocks in a short squeeze, and it makes puts dearer relative to calls.

counterparty risk.def: The risk that the other side of a contract fails to pay what it owes. For exchange-listed options it is carried by the clearinghouse; for over-the-counter contracts it stays with each side.

IV rank.def: Where today's implied volatility sits between its lowest and highest readings of the past 52 weeks, as a fraction of that range. Rare spikes stretch the range and pull the rank down.

IV percentile.def: The share of trading days in the past 52 weeks on which implied volatility was below today's level. It says how unusual today's level is among the days that actually occurred.

forward volatility.def: The implied volatility the market prices for the window between two expiries, found from the two expiries' implied volatilities because implied variance adds over time.

diagonal spread.def: A position that sells an option at one expiry and buys an option of the same type at a later expiry and a different strike. It is a calendar spread with the strikes moved apart.

put credit spread.def: A position that sells a put and buys a put with a lower strike on the same underlying and expiry, for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays above the sold strike, and its loss is capped by the bought put. Also called a bull put spread.

call credit spread.def: A position that sells a call and buys a call with a higher strike on the same underlying and expiry, for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays below the sold strike, and its loss is capped by the bought call. Also called a bear call spread.

LEAPS.def: Listed options with expiries more than a year away. The name stands for Long-term Equity AnticiPation Securities.
